summary: This memo defines a set of criteria for judging a DUA, a Directory User Agent, which is a program that lets people use a directory service. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a scoring sheet for programs that look things up in online phone books, so people can compare how good each one is.

questions: how to evaluate a directory user agent
how to evaluate directory user agents
subtitle: A scoring framework for evaluating X.500 Directory user interfaces

tldr.problem: X.500 Directory implementations varied widely in interface style, capabilities, and performance, making it hard to compare them or choose one for a particular use case.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a detailed questionnaire and scoring system covering 16 areas: hardware platforms, conformance to standards, interface design, query resolution performance, user-friendliness, and operational deployment.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can use the metrics to evaluate DUAs objectively, and DUA designers have clear criteria for comparing features. The metric system includes 'SearchStones'—a weighted formula measuring query efficiency.

facts.label: Test queries
facts.value: 11 named queries against Paul Barker's directory entry

today: RFC 1431 is informational and describes X.500 DUA evaluation metrics from 1993. X.500 was largely superseded by LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) in the late 1990s, and LDAP clients became the dominant directory user interface. However, the RFC remains historically relevant as documentation of X.500's evaluation approaches and as a reference for modern directory software assessment criteria.

sections.title: Directory User Agents and the Evaluation Problem
sections.content:
A DUA (Directory User Agent) is a program that lets users query an X.500 Directory—an online directory service designed by the OSI standards body. A DUA is the user interface layer; it translates a user's human-friendly search into technical X.500 protocol operations and displays the results.

DUAs come in many forms: some are terminal-based line-mode interfaces, others are graphical (X-Windows, MS-Windows, Macintosh), some run on a single machine, others split into a user interface and a server communicating over a network. Some are narrowly focused on finding people's email addresses and phone numbers; others are full-featured tools for managing directory data.

The RFC acknowledges that there is no universal 'best' DUA: a management tool is better for administrators; a simple lookup tool is better for casual users. However, some aspects are objectively measurable: Can the DUA actually find the entry you are looking for? How quickly? How many operations does it need to perform?

This RFC provides a detailed questionnaire and scoring system to evaluate DUAs across multiple dimensions, enabling informed comparison.
sections.eli5: Different phone-book programs are good for different jobs, but some are clearly faster or easier than others. This RFC is a test to measure how good each one is.

sections.title: The Evaluation Framework
sections.content:
The metrics are organized into 16 sections, each with questions worth points. Total points indicate overall capability.

  • General Information: Name, version, supplier, hardware and OS platforms, free or commercial, required dependencies.
  • OSI Conformance: Whether the DUA supports standard X.500 directory protocols (DAP), protocol stacks (TP over CONS, TP.4 over CLNS, TP over TCP/IP), and the full schema from X.520/X.521.
  • Research Community Standards: Support for COSINE/Internet Pilot extensions (RFC 1274, RFC 1277, OSI-DS standards).
  • General Style: Is it a 'white pages' interface (for finding people) or another type? Who is the target user (ordinary person, secretary, computer-literate user, manager, system administrator)? What terminal technology (scrolling, full-screen vt100, X-Windows, MS-Windows, Macintosh)?
  • Schema and DIT Structure: What object classes and attributes does it support? Is the DIT hierarchy rigid or flexible?
  • Query Entry: How does the user enter a query? Form filling, 'user-friendly names,' navigating the tree, or other?
  • Entry Location Strategy: Does it use searches, offers a list to select from, uses read-only operations, or combines strategies?
  • Results Display: Configurable attribute labels, local formatting options, multi-entry display, summary mode for faster display.
  • Association Handling: How is the directory access point configured? Automatic backup DSA failover, multiple connections, idle timeout handling, referral following, asynchronous operations.
  • Management Capabilities: Can it perform all directory operations? Can it manage system attributes (knowledge, replication info)? Can it add/modify/delete entries?
  • Query Resolution Efficiency: Measured using 'SearchStones'—a weighted metric combining bind, read, list, and search operations.
  • International Languages: Multi-lingual support, non-ASCII character handling.
  • User Friendliness: Runtime help, context-sensitive help, user-friendly error messages, syntax guidance for editing, browse capability.
  • Operational Use: Is the DUA widely deployed? Which pilots and organizations use it? Independent assessments available?
sections.eli5: The test has sections for hardware, features, speed, how you enter searches, how you see results, how easy it is to use, and whether real organizations actually use it.

sections.title: SearchStones: Measuring Query Efficiency
sections.content:
SearchStones is a weighted formula that measures the cost of resolving a directory query. It is not a timing measurement; rather, it counts and weights the underlying X.500 operations the DUA must perform.

The weight scheme is:

  • Bind (connect to directory server): 5 points
  • Read operation (direct lookup with an exact distinguished name): 1 point
  • List operation (enumerate children of a node): 2 points
  • Search at one level for countries, organizations, or localities: 3 points
  • Search at one level for organizational units, people, or roles: 3 points
  • Subtree search (across multiple directory levels): 5 points

For each test query, the RFC specifies 11 example queries ranging from straightforward (e.g., 'NAME=Paul Barker, OU=Computer Science, O=University College London, C=GB') to difficult (partial names, misspellings, abbreviations like 'c=uk' instead of 'c=GB'). Each query is scored with points if it succeeds in finding the author's entry, and a SearchStone rating for efficiency.

Low SearchStones indicate efficient queries; high SearchStones indicate the DUA is doing extensive searching. There is no universal 'good' score because the underlying X.500 network and DSA implementations vary, but the metric allows comparison between DUAs on the same network.
sections.eli5: The test measures how much work the phone-book program does to find someone: fewer operations are better, so different DUAs can be compared fairly.

sections.title: Interface Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC notes that DUAs make very different architectural choices, each with trade-offs:

  • Query entry: Form-filling is learnable but slower; 'user-friendly naming' is faster but harder for novices; navigating the DIT tree is intuitive for some, frustrating for others. There is no objectively best approach.
  • DIT representation: Some DUAs emphasize the hierarchical tree structure (good for administrators, confusing for casual users). Others hide the hierarchy and make the Directory appear like a flat database (good for casual users, limiting for complex queries).
  • Localization: DUAs can display attribute names and values in local languages and formats (e.g., showing phone numbers as extensions instead of full international dialing codes). This is highly valued but requires configuration per site.
  • Results presentation: Quick synopses (small set of attributes returned initially, larger set on demand) improve performance; multi-result display lets users compare entries.
  • Handling unknown attributes: When a DUA encounters an attribute in the directory that it doesn't recognize, it can ignore it, warn the user, or display the raw bytes. Different DUAs choose differently.

The RFC's approach to scoring reflects this diversity: points are awarded for capabilities, but points themselves do not determine whether a DUA is 'good' for a specific use case.
sections.eli5: Programs can be fast but hard to use, or easy but slow. The test measures different qualities separately so you can pick what matters for your job.

sections.title: Practical Deployment and Caveats
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that SearchStone ratings are not absolute performance measurements and should be interpreted with care. Factors affecting the real-world performance of a DUA include:

  • DIT structure and content: Real directories vary in depth, breadth, replication strategy, and attribute values. A DUA efficient in one directory may be inefficient in another.
  • DSA implementation diversity: At the time of writing, most DSAs (X.500 directory servers) were Quipu implementations, but this was changing. Different implementations have different performance characteristics.
  • Network topology and replication: Different directory domains use different replication strategies, affecting whether a query triggers a remote referral or can be answered locally.
  • Test query specificity: The RFC's test queries are limited to searching for a single author's entry (Paul Barker at University College London). The DIT structure around that entry is representative of much of the current directory, but not universal.

The RFC encourages testing directly against the target DSA to normalize results as much as possible. For broad comparisons across DUAs, the metrics are a useful starting point, but should be supplemented by real testing in your actual directory environment.

Organizations using the metrics should note that a high point score indicates broad capabilities, not necessarily suitability for their specific task. A DUA with lower management points may be ideal for a 'white pages' deployment; one with high management points may be overkill and harder to learn.
sections.eli5: The measurements show what each program can do, but how fast it actually is depends on your specific phone book and how you set it up.
